stances.claim: PBBM should use the one-month window before his January China visit to diplomatically secure Chinese cooperation on EEZ resource extraction -- within constitutional limits and 'without yielding the arbitral gains we already won' -- because this is the path to alleviating poverty and energizing power plants with cleaner and cheaper electricity.
stances.rhetorical_move: diplomatic-window prescription with dual constraints (constitution + AA)

stances.claim: The reported MOU compromise language -- 'oil and gas operations shall be subject to the laws of the Philippines' plus the non-renunciation clause for either party's SCS claims -- satisfies the PH Constitution because (1) EDU remains under 'full control and supervision of the State' with the 60% Filipino-capital rule for co-production/joint-venture partners, and (2) the President may enter foreign technical/financial assistance agreements for large-scale petroleum/oil EDU.

China's cooperation is 'very important, nay, indispensable' for any practical EEZ extraction because China retains 'effective military control over the SCS' despite US freedom-of-navigation sailings, and 'no private concessionaire will dare invest billions of dollars and operate in the SCS without China's assurance of no interference and no swarming.'

Given China's past willingness to assist and cooperate, PH should resume the past initiatives and forge an MOU to harness private concessionaires for EEZ extraction -- modeled on the Shell-Malampaya service contract (2001-2022) that yielded over $13 billion in cash to government from its 60% gross-earnings share and 3,400 MW of clean electricity (~25% of PH requirements).

Malampaya natural gas will be exhausted in 2024; with Chinese cooperation, government and/or private concessionaires can continue receiving cash and clean energy from areas near Malampaya and the new oil fields known as SC 72 and SC 75 -- making the MOU not merely about past initiatives but about replacing imminently-exhausting energy infrastructure.

notable_anecdotes: PBBM's own framing -- that the EEZ resources are a 'small matter to China [which] for us, is something huge. So, we need to fight for it and benefit from it...' -- quoted to anchor the column in the President's own asymmetric-stakes framing.
The 'ON, BELOW, and ABOVE our EEZ' three-dimensional formulation of the AA's grant -- making explicit the spatial scope of the sovereign rights affirmed (water column, seabed, airspace).

The visceral contrast between Chinese 'military fortresses, airfields, and missile silos' and PH 'fishermen's ancient, motorized cascos' -- the column's most vivid image, mobilizing the asymmetric-power tableau without naming a specific incident.

The reported MOU compromise text quoted nearly verbatim -- 'shall not be interpreted as a renunciation by either party of any right relating to the (SCS), or a recognition of or support for the other party's position with regard to any claim relating to the area' -- making the legal-fiction architecture of joint development concrete.

DFA's February 2022 termination 'aware of the impending change in the administration' -- the diplomatic-pause-as-handover-courtesy detail that explains why PBBM is starting from where Duterte stopped rather than where Duterte ended.

The Malampaya scoreboard -- '$13 billion in cash from its 60 percent share of the gross earnings' over 2001-2022 plus '3,400 megawatts of clean electricity -- roughly one-fourth of our country's requirements' -- converting an abstract service-contract precedent into auditable national-revenue arithmetic.
The naming of next-field opportunities -- 'SC 72 and 75' -- making the post-Malampaya pipeline concrete rather than aspirational.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban opens on President Bongbong Marcos Jr.'s frustration at China's intransigence in blocking the previous administration's effort to extract oil and gas from the PH exclusive economic zone in the South China Sea -- PBBM warning the government may abandon government-to-government talks and 'find other ways' because what is a 'small matter to China... for us, is something huge.' With PBBM visiting China in January 2023, the new administration has one month to diplomatically secure Chinese cooperation 'within the limits prescribed by our Constitution and without yielding the arbitral gains we already won.' The July 2016 Arbitral Award recognized PH sovereign rights to explore, develop, and utilize (EDU) resources under its EEZ -- ON, BELOW, and ABOVE -- but did not grant sovereignty over LAND areas in the SCS; China rejects the AA, claims almost the entire SCS by historic title, has reclaimed features into 'military fortresses, airfields, and missile silos,' and uses its Coast Guard and militia to swarm 'puny military vessels' and 'fishermen's ancient, motorized cascos.' Nevertheless, China has agreed in principle to 'joint developments' -- requiring first a government-to-government MOU, then private commercial concessionaires for financial, technical, and management implementation. Quietly, Chinese and Philippine diplomats had negotiated for three years; the reported compromise language -- that 'the oil and gas operations shall be subject to the laws of the Philippines' with a non-renunciation clause preserving both parties' SCS claims -- satisfies Article XII of the PH Constitution because EDU stays under 'full control and supervision of the State,' the 60% Filipino-capital rule applies to joint-venture partners, and the President may enter foreign technical/financial assistance agreements for large-scale petroleum EDU. DFA terminated negotiations in February 2022 to give the incoming administration a free hand. CJ argues Chinese cooperation is 'very important, nay, indispensable' because China retains 'effective military control over the SCS' despite US freedom-of-navigation sailings, and 'no private concessionaire will dare invest billions of dollars and operate in the SCS without China's assurance of no interference and no swarming.' The Shell-Malampaya service contract (2001-2022) is the model: $13 billion in cash to government from its 60% gross-earnings share and 3,400 MW of clean electricity (~25% of national requirement). With Malampaya gas exhausting in 2024, Chinese cooperation could enable continued extraction from areas nearby and from new oil fields 'known as SC 72 and 75' in the EEZ.
